q: For a railway work proposal to be financially justified, the minimum expected rate of return on the initial estimated cost is generally:
e: Under the railway financial code, a remunerative work must show an expected return of at least 10% on its initial estimated (capital) cost; proposals below this threshold are not treated as financially justified.

q: The Payback Period method of capital appraisal suffers from the limitation that it:

options.B: Ignores the time value of money and cash flows after the payback period
options.C: Requires the cost of capital as an input
options.D: Considers the entire life of the project

e: Payback counts only the cash inflows needed to recover the outlay; it ignores discounting (time value of money) and all inflows arising after the payback point, so long-life profitable projects may be undervalued.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Financial Internal Rate of Return (FIRR) measures the return to the Railways from the project.
2. Economic Internal Rate of Return (EIRR) also takes into account social and external benefits.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
e: Both statements are correct: FIRR uses only the financial cash flows accruing to the Railways, while EIRR is computed on economic costs and benefits, including social and external effects on the economy.

q: Where residential quarters form part of a larger scheme, financial justification requires that the assessed rent should yield a return of at least:
e: Residential buildings forming part of a larger scheme are treated as remunerative only if the assessed rent is expected to yield at least 6% return on the capital cost of the quarters.

q: A product has fixed costs of Rs 2,00,000 and a P/V ratio of 40%. Its break-even sales are:
e: Break-even sales = Fixed cost / P/V ratio = 2,00,000 / 0.40 = Rs 5,00,000, the sales level at which contribution exactly covers the fixed cost.

q: The P/V (Profit-Volume) ratio is computed as:

options.A: Profit divided by Sales, multiplied by 100
options.B: Contribution divided by Sales, multiplied by 100
options.C: Sales divided by Variable Cost, multiplied by 100
options.D: Fixed Cost divided by Contribution, multiplied by 100

e: P/V ratio = Contribution / Sales x 100; it shows the proportion of each rupee of sales available to cover fixed cost and provide profit.

q: In PERT, if the optimistic time is 10 days, most likely time is 15 days and pessimistic time is 25 days, the expected time is approximately:
e: PERT expected time te = (10 + 4 x 15 + 25) / 6 = 95 / 6 = about 15.8, i.e., approximately 16 days.

q: The Current Ratio of an enterprise primarily measures its:
e: The current ratio (current assets / current liabilities) shows whether short-term obligations can be met from short-term assets, so it measures short-term liquidity.

q: Zero-Based Budgeting requires that:

options.A: The budget of the previous year is adopted without change
options.B: Every item of expenditure is justified afresh, as if it were a new proposal, in each budget cycle
options.C: No budget is prepared for revenue expenditure

e: In zero-based budgeting no item is accepted merely because it existed last year; every item of expenditure must be justified afresh, as if new, in each budget cycle.

q: In the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) technique of project appraisal, future cash flows are:

options.A: Taken at their face value without adjustment
options.B: Discounted to their present value using an appropriate discount rate
options.D: Considered only for the first five years

e: DCF recognises the time value of money: each future inflow and outflow is multiplied by a present-value factor at the chosen discount rate so that all flows are compared at today's value.

q: Which of the following works is generally exempt from the requirement of financial justification?
e: Safety works are undertaken to protect life and property and are exempt from financial justification; remunerative works like new lines, crossing stations and doublings must pass the return test.

q:
Consider the following statements regarding exceptions to financial justification:
1. Passenger amenity works and labour welfare works do not require financial justification.
2. If an exempt item forms part of a larger scheme, the whole scheme must be financially justified.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
e: Both statements are correct: passenger amenity and labour welfare works are exempt categories, but if such an exempt item forms part of a larger scheme, the whole scheme must be financially justified.

q: Modified Economic Internal Rate of Return (MEIRR), as compared to EIRR, additionally takes into account:

options.C: Only the cash receipts of the Railways
options.D: The book value of assets at the end of project life

e: MEIRR modifies the economic appraisal by also bringing in the network (system-wide) effects of the project, such as benefits arising on connected routes, which a project-wise EIRR may miss.

q: In the economic appraisal of a project, taxes and subsidies are excluded from EIRR computation because they are treated as:
e: Taxes and subsidies merely transfer purchasing power within the economy without consuming real resources, so in economic appraisal they are excluded as transfer payments, though they count in financial appraisal.

q: The Internal Rate of Return (IRR) of a project is the discount rate at which:

options.A: The total cash inflows equal the initial investment
options.B: The Net Present Value of the project is zero
options.C: The payback period is the shortest

e: IRR is the discount rate at which the present value of cash inflows exactly equals the outlay, i.e., NPV is zero; a project is acceptable if its IRR exceeds the cut-off rate.

q: The Average Rate of Return (ARR) method of project appraisal is based on:

options.A: Cash flows discounted at the cost of capital
options.B: Average accounting profit as a percentage of investment
options.C: Cumulative cash recovery of the initial outlay

e: ARR = Average annual accounting profit / Investment x 100; it uses book profits (after depreciation) rather than cash flows and ignores the time value of money.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Both ARR and Payback are traditional methods that ignore the time value of money.
2. The DCF technique recognises the time value of money.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
e: Both statements are correct: ARR and payback are traditional non-discounting methods, while the DCF technique discounts future cash flows and so recognises the time value of money.

q: The Net Present Value (NPV) of a project is computed as:

options.A: Total undiscounted cash inflows minus the initial cost
options.B: Present value of cash inflows minus the present value of cash outflows (initial cost)
options.C: Initial cost divided by annual cash inflow
options.D: Accounting profit multiplied by the present-worth factor

e: NPV = Present value of cash inflows minus the present value of cash outflows (initial cost); a positive NPV means the project earns more than the discount (hurdle) rate.

q: The present-worth factor (PWF) is used in project appraisal to:

options.A: Convert a future amount into its present value
options.B: Convert a present amount into its future value
options.D: Work out the average rate of return

e: The present-worth (present value) factor converts a sum receivable or payable at a future date into its equivalent value today at the given discount rate.

q: Viability Gap Funding (VGF) is associated with:

options.B: Public-Private Partnership projects that are economically justified but not fully financially viable

e: VGF is capital grant support given to PPP projects which are economically justified but whose revenues (user charges) alone cannot make them fully financially viable.

q: Lease financing and market borrowings raised for railway projects through institutions like IRFC are broadly covered under:
e: Lease financing and market borrowings routed through institutions like IRFC are resources raised outside the budget, hence they are grouped under Extra Budgetary Resources (EBR).

q: In management accounting, 'contribution' is equal to:
e: Contribution = Sales - Variable cost; it is the amount available first to meet fixed costs and thereafter to provide profit.

q: At the break-even point, the total contribution is exactly equal to:
e: At the break-even point there is no profit and no loss, so the total contribution earned is exactly absorbed by the total fixed cost.

q: A firm sells a product for Rs 200 per unit. Variable cost is Rs 120 per unit and fixed costs are Rs 4,00,000. The break-even point in units is:
e: Contribution per unit = 200 - 120 = Rs 80; Break-even point = Fixed cost / Contribution per unit = 4,00,000 / 80 = 5,000 units.

q: Sales are Rs 10,00,000 and variable costs are Rs 6,00,000. The P/V ratio is:
If the P/V ratio is 25% and fixed costs are Rs 3,00,000, the break-even sales are:
e: Break-even sales = Fixed cost / P/V ratio = 3,00,000 / 0.25 = Rs 12,00,000.

q: A machine costs Rs 5,00,000 and generates a net cash inflow of Rs 1,25,000 per year. Its payback period is:
e: Payback period = Initial cost / Annual net cash inflow = 5,00,000 / 1,25,000 = 4 years.

q: A project costing Rs 1,00,000 yields a cash inflow of Rs 60,000 at the end of the first year. At a discount rate of 10%, the present value of this inflow is approximately:
e: Present value = 60,000 x 1/(1.10) = 60,000 x 0.909 = approximately Rs 54,545.

q: The margin of safety in break-even analysis is:

options.D: Fixed cost divided by P/V ratio

e: Margin of safety = Actual sales - Break-even sales; it shows by how much sales can fall before the firm reaches the no-profit-no-loss point.

q: Current assets are Rs 6,00,000 and current liabilities are Rs 3,00,000. The current ratio is:
e: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities = 6,00,000 / 3,00,000 = 2 : 1.

q: Current assets are Rs 8,00,000, inventory is Rs 3,00,000 and current liabilities are Rs 2,50,000. The quick (liquid) ratio is:
e: Quick assets = Current assets - Inventory = 8,00,000 - 3,00,000 = Rs 5,00,000; Quick ratio = 5,00,000 / 2,50,000 = 2 : 1.

q: Share capital is Rs 4,00,000 and long-term debt is Rs 2,00,000. The debt-equity ratio is:
e: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debt / Share capital = 2,00,000 / 4,00,000 = 0.5 : 1.

q: Net profit after tax is Rs 2,00,000 and capital employed is Rs 10,00,000. The Return on Investment (ROI) is:
e: ROI = Net profit after tax / Capital employed x 100 = 2,00,000 / 10,00,000 x 100 = 20%.

q: A railway earned gross traffic receipts of Rs 2,00,000 crore against ordinary working expenses of Rs 1,90,000 crore. Its Operating Ratio is:
e: Operating Ratio = Ordinary working expenses / Gross traffic receipts x 100 = 1,90,000 / 2,00,000 x 100 = 95%.

q: The inventory turnover ratio is computed as:

options.A: Average inventory divided by cost of goods sold
options.B: Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory

e: Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of goods sold / Average inventory; it shows how many times the stock is sold and replaced during a period.

q: Which of the following is a solvency ratio?
e: The debt-equity ratio compares long-term debt with owners' funds and so measures long-term solvency; the current ratio measures liquidity and the turnover ratios measure activity.

q: The interest coverage ratio indicates:

options.A: The number of times interest is covered by profit before interest and tax
options.B: The proportion of debt in total capital
options.C: The liquidity available for paying interest in cash only
options.D: The rate of interest payable on borrowings

e: Interest coverage ratio = Profit before interest and tax / Interest; it shows how many times the fixed interest charge is covered by earnings, indicating the safety of lenders.

q: The proprietary ratio expresses the relationship between:
e: Proprietary ratio = Proprietors' funds / Total assets; it expresses the proportion of the total assets financed by the owners' funds.

q: A fund flow statement is primarily concerned with changes in:
e: A fund flow statement explains the causes of change in working capital (current assets minus current liabilities) between two balance sheet dates.

q: Which of the following is a source of funds in a fund flow statement?
e: Funds from operations is a source of funds; purchase of fixed assets, repayment of long-term loans and payment of dividend are applications (uses) of funds.

q: A cash flow statement differs from a fund flow statement in that the cash flow statement focuses on changes in:
e: The cash flow statement tracks movements in cash and cash equivalents only, whereas the fund flow statement tracks the broader concept of funds, i.e., working capital.

q: Under responsibility accounting, a 'cost centre' is a responsibility centre whose manager is accountable for:
e: A cost centre's manager controls and is accountable only for the costs incurred in that centre; revenues belong to revenue centres and profits to profit centres.

q: In variance analysis, a material price variance arises due to the difference between:

options.A: Standard quantity and actual quantity consumed
options.B: Standard price and actual price paid for materials

e: Material price variance arises from the difference between the standard price and the actual price paid, applied to the quantity purchased or consumed; quantity differences give the usage variance.

q: Sensitivity analysis in project appraisal is used to examine:

options.A: The effect of changes in key variables on the project's viability/return
options.B: The sequence of activities in a project network
options.C: The allocation of overheads to cost centres
options.D: The liquidity position of the enterprise

e: Sensitivity analysis re-works the return or NPV by varying key inputs such as traffic, earnings, cost and completion time, to see how sensitive the project's viability is to changes in them.

q: In a make-or-buy decision, the most relevant cost consideration is:

options.A: The total cost including allocated fixed overheads
options.B: The incremental (avoidable) cost of making compared with the purchase price
options.D: The book value of the existing plant

e: Only costs that differ between alternatives are relevant: the incremental (avoidable) cost of making is compared with the purchase price; allocated fixed overheads and sunk costs do not change with the decision.

q: In PERT, the expected time of an activity with optimistic time 6 days, most likely time 9 days and pessimistic time 18 days is:
e: Expected time te = (6 + 4 x 9 + 18) / 6 = 60 / 6 = 10 days.

q: In a project network, the critical path is the:

options.B: Longest path through the network, determining the minimum project duration
options.C: Path with the maximum number of activities

e: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent activities in the network; its total time determines the minimum possible project duration and its activities have zero float.

q: A project network has three paths: A-B-D with duration 14 days, A-C-D with duration 19 days and A-C-E with duration 16 days. The project duration is:
e: Project duration is set by the longest path, A-C-D = 19 days; the shorter paths have float and cannot determine the completion date.

q:
Consider the following statements about PERT and CPM:
1. PERT is probabilistic and uses three time estimates.
2. CPM is deterministic and uses a single time estimate.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
e: Both statements are correct: PERT is probabilistic and uses three time estimates (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic), while CPM is deterministic and uses a single time estimate with time-cost trade-off.

q: 'Fully distributed cost' in traffic costing means the cost that includes:

options.A: Only the direct cost of carrying the traffic
options.B: Direct costs plus an allocated share of joint and common costs and overheads
options.C: Only the marginal cost of an additional unit of traffic
options.D: Only the fuel cost of train operations

e: Fully distributed cost loads a service with its direct cost plus an allocated share of joint and common costs and overheads, so that the entire cost of the railway is absorbed by the traffic carried.

q: Traffic costing on Indian Railways is mainly used for:

options.B: Pricing decisions and assessing the profitability of different streams of traffic
options.C: Preparing the annual budget estimates only

e: Traffic costing works out the unit cost of coaching and goods services (per PKM/NTKM), which is used for pricing decisions and for assessing the profitability of different streams of traffic.

q: Specific fuel consumption (SFC) in railway costing is generally expressed per:
e: SFC is expressed per 1000 GTKM because fuel consumption varies with the gross load hauled (including tare) over distance, making gross tonne kilometres the proper workload base.

q: Management accounting differs from financial accounting in that management accounting:

options.B: Is prepared mainly for internal management decision-making and is not statutory
options.C: Is audited by the C&AG in all cases
options.D: Records only past transactions for shareholders

e: Management accounting is prepared voluntarily for internal management decision-making and is not governed by statute, whereas financial accounting is statutory and mainly for external reporting.

q: On Indian Railways, the Finance Officer also functions as a management accountant primarily by:

options.A: Maintaining the statutory books of account only
options.B: Providing cost, budgetary and appraisal information to management for decision-making
options.C: Conducting the statutory audit of accounts

e: The Finance Officer functions as a management accountant by providing cost, budgetary and project appraisal information to management for planning, control and decision-making.

q: 'Standard cost' means:

options.A: The actual cost incurred in the previous year
options.B: A pre-determined cost based on technical estimates, used as a benchmark for control
options.C: The average cost of all products
options.D: The market price of the product

e: Standard cost is a pre-determined cost based on technical estimates of an efficient level of performance, used as a benchmark against which actual costs are compared for control.

q: Joint costs are costs that are:

options.B: Common to two or more products or services up to the split-off point
options.C: Charged only to the main product

e: Joint costs are common to two or more products up to the split-off point, where the products become separately identifiable; they must be apportioned among the joint products.

q: The materiality concept in accounting implies that:

options.A: All transactions, however small, must be recorded separately
options.B: Only items significant enough to influence decisions need separate attention/disclosure
options.C: Material costs alone are relevant for decisions
options.D: Immaterial items should never be recorded

e: Under the materiality concept, only items significant enough to influence decisions need separate attention or disclosure; insignificant items may be grouped or treated approximately.

q: Which of the following is an activity (efficiency) ratio?
e: Debtors turnover ratio (credit sales / average debtors) measures the efficiency of receivables collection, an activity ratio; the others are solvency, profitability and liquidity ratios.

q: The operating ratio of a railway improves (becomes more favourable) when:

options.A: Working expenses rise faster than earnings
options.B: Earnings increase with a proportionately smaller increase in working expenses
options.C: Both earnings and expenses fall equally

e: Operating ratio = Working expenses / Earnings x 100; it falls (improves) when earnings increase with a proportionately smaller increase in working expenses.

q: Under the BOOT model of project execution, the letters B-O-O-T stand for:
e: BOOT stands for Build, Own, Operate and Transfer: the concessionaire builds the facility, owns and operates it during the concession, and then transfers it to the authority.

q: 'Gross working capital' refers to:

options.B: The total of all current assets of an enterprise
options.C: The total of all current liabilities of an enterprise

e: Gross working capital means the total of all current assets of an enterprise; current assets minus current liabilities gives net working capital.

q: A product is sold for Rs 50 per unit. Its variable cost is Rs 30 per unit and the fixed costs are Rs 2,40,000. The break-even point in units is:
e: Contribution per unit = 50 - 30 = Rs 20; Break-even point = 2,40,000 / 20 = 12,000 units.

q: The operating cycle of an enterprise is the period between:

options.A: Cash outlay on raw materials and other inputs and the realisation of cash from the sale of finished goods (through debtors)
options.C: Sanction of the budget and its final approval
options.D: Placement of an order for materials and their receipt in stores

e: The operating cycle runs from the cash outlay on raw materials and other inputs, through production, stock and credit sales (debtors), to the realisation of cash from the sale of finished goods.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 12,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 5,00,000. Its working capital is:
e: Working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities = 12,00,000 - 5,00,000 = Rs 7,00,000.

q: Budgetary control essentially means:

options.A: Preparation of budgets by the Budget section
options.B: Establishment of budgets and continuous comparison of actual results with them, so that corrective action can be taken
options.C: Control over the staff of the accounts office
options.D: Restricting expenditure to the lowest possible level

e: Budgetary control means establishing budgets with assigned responsibilities, continuously comparing actual results with them, analysing variances and taking corrective action - not merely preparing the budgets.

q: An enterprise records the following: Sales Rs 5,00,000 with profit Rs 50,000 in Year 1, and Sales Rs 7,00,000 with profit Rs 1,10,000 in Year 2. The P/V ratio is:
e: With fixed cost unchanged, P/V ratio = Change in profit / Change in sales = (1,10,000 - 50,000) / (7,00,000 - 5,00,000) = 60,000 / 2,00,000 = 30%.

q: A flexible budget is a budget which:

options.A: Remains unchanged whatever the level of activity
options.B: Is prepared for a single fixed level of activity only
options.C: Is designed to change in accordance with the level of activity actually attained
options.D: Can be prepared at any time during the year

e: A flexible budget is designed to change in accordance with the level of activity actually attained, by separating fixed and variable costs, so it can be compared fairly with actual results.

q: Fixed costs are Rs 5,00,000 and the P/V ratio is 50%. The sales required to earn a desired profit of Rs 2,50,000 are:
e: Sales for desired profit = (Fixed cost + Desired profit) / P/V ratio = (5,00,000 + 2,50,000) / 0.50 = Rs 15,00,000.

q: The master budget of an enterprise is:

options.B: The summarised budget incorporating all functional budgets, in the form of a budgeted profit and loss account and balance sheet
options.D: The budget of capital works only

e: The master budget is the summarised budget incorporating all functional budgets, presented as a budgeted profit and loss account and balance sheet for the enterprise as a whole.

q: A sunk cost is:

options.A: A cost that varies directly with output
options.B: A future cost that can still be avoided
options.C: The benefit expected from the best alternative use of a resource
options.D: A cost already incurred in the past which cannot be recovered and is irrelevant for future decisions

e: A sunk cost is a cost already incurred in the past which cannot be recovered; being the same under all future alternatives, it is irrelevant for future decisions.

q: A product sells for Rs 80 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 50 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 3,00,000. The number of units to be sold to earn a target profit of Rs 90,000 is:
e: Contribution per unit = 80 - 50 = Rs 30; Units for target profit = (Fixed cost + Target profit) / Contribution per unit = (3,00,000 + 90,000) / 30 = 13,000 units.

q: Opportunity cost means:

options.A: The benefit forgone by not using a resource in its next best alternative use
options.B: The total cost of materials purchased
options.C: A cost that has already been incurred and cannot be changed
options.D: The difference between fixed cost and variable cost

e: Opportunity cost is the benefit forgone by not using a resource in its next best alternative use; it is a notional cost relevant to decisions involving scarce resources.

q: Actual sales of an enterprise are Rs 8,00,000 and its break-even sales are Rs 5,00,000. Its margin of safety as a percentage of actual sales is:
e: Margin of safety = 8,00,000 - 5,00,000 = Rs 3,00,000; as a percentage of actual sales = 3,00,000 / 8,00,000 x 100 = 37.5%.

q: Marginal cost is best defined as:

options.A: Total fixed cost divided by the units produced
options.B: The average cost per unit at the current level of output
options.C: The total cost of all units produced in a period
options.D: The change in total cost resulting from producing one additional unit of output

e: Marginal cost is the change in total cost resulting from producing one additional unit of output; in practice it comprises the variable elements of cost.

q: Under the Net Present Value method, a project should be accepted when:

options.A: Its NPV is less than zero
options.B: Its NPV is exactly equal to the initial investment
options.C: Its NPV is positive, i.e., the present value of cash inflows exceeds the initial outlay
options.D: The cash inflows are the highest among all alternatives, ignoring discounting

e: Under NPV, a project is accepted when its NPV is positive, i.e., the present value of cash inflows, discounted at the cost of capital, exceeds the initial outlay.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 1,50,000. Its cash inflows are Rs 80,000 at the end of Year 1 (present value factor 0.909) and Rs 1,00,000 at the end of Year 2 (present value factor 0.826). The Net Present Value of the project is:
Semi-variable costs are costs which:

options.A: Remain constant in total at all levels of output
options.B: Are partly fixed and partly variable, e.g., telephone charges comprising a fixed rental plus call charges
options.C: Vary in direct proportion to output
options.D: Are incurred only in abnormal years

e: Semi-variable costs are partly fixed and partly variable, e.g., telephone charges comprising a fixed rental plus charges varying with calls made.

q: A project costing Rs 3,00,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 1,00,000 in Year 1, Rs 1,50,000 in Year 2 and Rs 1,00,000 in Year 3. Its payback period is:
e: Cumulative inflows: Year 1 Rs 1,00,000 and Year 2 Rs 2,50,000; the remaining Rs 50,000 is recovered from half of Year 3's inflow, so payback = 2 + 0.5 = 2.5 years.

q: The Profitability Index of a project is:

options.A: The initial investment divided by the present value of cash inflows
options.B: The NPV divided by the annual sales
options.C: The present value of future cash inflows divided by the initial investment; a project is acceptable if the index is greater than 1
options.D: The annual accounting profit divided by the initial investment

e: Profitability Index = Present value of future cash inflows / Initial investment; an index greater than 1 means NPV is positive and the project is acceptable.

q: An investment of Rs 4,00,000 is expected to yield an average annual profit (after depreciation and tax) of Rs 60,000. The Average Rate of Return on the initial investment is:
e: ARR on initial investment = Average annual profit / Initial investment x 100 = 60,000 / 4,00,000 x 100 = 15%.

q: The discounted payback period is:

options.A: The time required to recover the initial investment from the discounted (present) values of the cash inflows
options.B: The payback period computed after deducting tax from the inflows
options.C: The payback period of a project purchased at a discount
options.D: The period over which depreciation is charged on the asset

e: The discounted payback period is the time required to recover the initial investment from the discounted (present) values of the cash inflows, thus recognising the time value of money.

q: In standard costing, a variance is said to be 'favourable' (in respect of a cost item) when:

options.A: The actual cost is more than the standard cost
options.B: More material is consumed than the standard quantity
options.C: The actual price paid is more than the standard price
options.D: The actual cost is less than the standard cost

e: For a cost item, a variance is favourable when the actual cost is less than the standard cost, e.g., paying a lower price or consuming less material than standard.

q: The standard quantity of material for actual output is 500 kg, but the actual quantity consumed is 550 kg. The standard price is Rs 20 per kg. The material usage variance is:
e: Material usage variance = (Standard quantity - Actual quantity) x Standard price = (500 - 550) x 20 = Rs 1,000 (Adverse), because more material was consumed than the standard allows.

q: In DCF appraisal, the cut-off (hurdle) rate used for judging the acceptability of a project is generally the:

options.A: Bank rate announced by the RBI
options.B: Cost of capital of the enterprise
options.C: Rate of depreciation charged on the assets
options.D: Interest rate paid on the last loan raised

e: In DCF appraisal the cut-off (hurdle) rate is generally the cost of capital of the enterprise - the minimum return a project must earn to be acceptable.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 6,400 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 25 and the carrying cost is Rs 2 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:
The Economic Order Quantity is the order size at which:

options.A: The ordering cost alone is the minimum possible
options.B: The total of ordering costs and carrying costs is the minimum (the two costs being equal)
options.D: The lead time for supplies is the shortest

e: At the EOQ, the annual ordering cost and the annual carrying cost are equal, so the total of ordering and carrying costs is at its minimum.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 6,00,000 and the interest payable is Rs 1,50,000. The interest coverage ratio is:
e: Interest coverage ratio = Profit before interest and tax / Interest = 6,00,000 / 1,50,000 = 4 times.

q: In PERT, the expected time (te) of an activity, where TO is the optimistic time, TM the most likely time and TP the pessimistic time, is computed as:
e: In PERT the expected time is a weighted average giving the most likely time a weight of 4: te = (TO + 4TM + TP) / 6.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 9,00,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,50,000. The debtors turnover ratio is:
e: Debtors turnover ratio = Credit sales / Average debtors = 9,00,000 / 1,50,000 = 6 times.

q: In a project network, the total float of the activities lying on the critical path is:
e: Activities on the critical path have no slack: any delay in them delays the whole project, so their total float is zero.

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 8,00,000 and its average inventory is Rs 1,60,000. The inventory turnover ratio is:
e: Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of goods sold / Average inventory = 8,00,000 / 1,60,000 = 5 times.

q: 'Crashing' in project network analysis means:

options.B: Reducing the project duration by incurring additional cost on critical activities
options.C: Increasing the number of activities in the network
options.D: Preparing a revised estimate after the project has failed

e: Crashing means reducing the project duration by incurring additional cost (extra resources, overtime) on critical activities, accepting higher cost for earlier completion.

q: The net profit after tax of a company is Rs 5,00,000 and the preference dividend payable is Rs 50,000. If the company has 90,000 equity shares, its Earnings Per Share (EPS) is:
e: EPS = (Net profit after tax - Preference dividend) / Number of equity shares = (5,00,000 - 50,000) / 90,000 = Rs 5.00 per share.

q: A 'cost unit' is:

options.A: A unit of product or service in relation to which costs are ascertained, e.g., cost per tonne-kilometre
options.B: A section of the factory where costs are collected
options.C: The total cost of a department for a period
options.D: A unit of currency used in the cost accounts

e: A cost unit is the unit of product or service in relation to which costs are ascertained, e.g., cost per tonne-kilometre; a cost centre, by contrast, is where costs are collected.

q: A major limitation of traffic costing based on fully distributed cost is that:

options.A: It does not record fuel consumption
options.B: It cannot be applied to coaching traffic
options.C: The apportionment of joint and common costs among different services is necessarily arbitrary, so the results are approximate
options.D: It ignores the earnings of the railway altogether

e: Fully distributed costing requires joint and common costs to be apportioned among services on some chosen basis; this apportionment is necessarily arbitrary, so the resulting costs are only approximate.

q: The fixed assets turnover ratio is computed as:

options.A: Net fixed assets divided by net sales
options.B: Net sales divided by net fixed assets
options.C: Total sales divided by total assets
options.D: Net fixed assets divided by capital employed

e: Fixed assets turnover ratio = Net sales / Net fixed assets; it measures how efficiently the investment in fixed assets is used to generate sales.

q: On Indian Railways, 'Return on Capital' is worked out as the net earnings expressed as a percentage of:
e: On Indian Railways, Return on Capital is the net earnings expressed as a percentage of the capital-at-charge, i.e., the capital actually invested in the railway undertaking.

q: In a break-even chart, the 'angle of incidence' is the angle formed at the break-even point between:

options.A: The sales line and the total cost line; a wider angle indicates a higher rate of profit earning
options.B: The fixed cost line and the sales line
options.C: The total cost line and the horizontal axis only
options.D: The sales line and the vertical axis

e: The angle of incidence is formed at the break-even point between the sales line and the total cost line; a wider angle indicates a higher rate of profit earning beyond break-even.

q: IRPSM (Indian Railways Project Sanction and Management) is:

options.A: A financial institution that lends to the Railways
options.B: A portal for procurement of stores
options.C: The web-based system used for submission, examination, sanction and monitoring of project proposals in the works programme
options.D: A committee that fixes freight rates

e: IRPSM is the web-based system used on Indian Railways for submission, examination, sanction and monitoring of project proposals included in the works programme.

q: In infrastructure projects executed through PPP, an SPV (Special Purpose Vehicle) is:

options.A: A type of wagon used for project materials
options.B: A separate entity created specifically to undertake and finance a particular project
options.C: A method of valuing railway assets
options.D: A fund maintained by the Railway Board for works

e: An SPV is a separate entity created specifically to undertake and finance a particular project, keeping the project's assets, liabilities and risks distinct from those of the promoters.
